title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 4
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain noticed that its properties displaying a prominent 'guest favourite' badge on booking sites receive higher average review scores than properties without the badge. The chain plans to apply for the badge at all its properties in order to raise their review scores.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the plan?
options: A. Some guests do not read badges before booking.
B. The badge appears in a different colour on mobile devices.
C. Properties with the badge charge slightly higher rates.
D. The badge is awarded by the booking site on the basis of a property's existing review scores.
E. Review scores across the industry have risen in recent years.
questions.explanation: The badge is an effect of high scores, not a cause, so applying for it cannot raise them — there is nothing to apply for that is not already earned. D and E describe correlates that leave the causal direction untouched.

questions.prompt: A dairy cooperative reports that herds fed a new supplement produced 9 per cent more milk than herds on the standard feed during the trial period. The cooperative recommends the supplement to all its members on that basis.
questions.question: The recommendation depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. The supplement is manufactured within the cooperative's region.
B. Milk prices will remain stable in the coming year.
C. The additional milk is worth more than the additional cost of the supplement.
D. The herds in the trial were the cooperative's largest.
E. No member currently uses a different supplement.
questions.explanation: A production gain is a reason to adopt only if it is worth what it costs; without that, a 9 per cent yield increase can still lose money. C bears on the size of the benefit but is not required for the recommendation to make sense.

questions.prompt: In the years after a national campaign encouraged cyclists to wear helmets, the number of cyclists admitted to hospital with head injuries fell by 30 per cent. Campaign organisers cite this as evidence that helmets prevent head injuries.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the organisers' reasoning?
options: A. Helmets are more effective in low-speed falls than in collisions with vehicles.
B. Some cyclists wear helmets incorrectly.
C. Hospital admission criteria were unchanged during the period.
D. Head injuries among pedestrians did not change.
E. The total number of cycle journeys made fell by roughly 30 per cent over the same period.
questions.explanation: If cycling itself fell by the same proportion, injuries per journey are unchanged and the campaign may have reduced cycling rather than injury risk. D removes a rival explanation; A concerns the size of the protective effect, not the inference.

questions.prompt: A call centre introduced a training programme and found that agents who completed it resolved customer queries in less time than agents who had not. Management concluded that the training makes agents more efficient.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen management's conclusion?
options: A. Agents chose for themselves whether to attend the training.
B. Agents were assigned to the training in the order their employee numbers happened to fall, and the two groups had equal average resolution times beforehand.
C. The training was designed by an external consultancy.
D. Customer satisfaction scores also rose during the period.
E. The training programme cost less than management expected.
questions.explanation: Assignment unrelated to ability plus equal baselines is what rules out the obvious confound. A would weaken it badly; D is consistent with the conclusion but does not address selection.

questions.prompt: Every apple variety stored in the Kesteven cooperative's controlled-atmosphere rooms keeps for at least six months. Some varieties the cooperative grows are not stored in those rooms. All varieties that keep for at least six months are sold in the winter market.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Every variety stored in the controlled-atmosphere rooms is sold in the winter market.
B. Every variety the cooperative grows is sold in the winter market.
C. No variety kept outside the rooms is sold in the winter market.
D. Most of the cooperative's varieties keep for at least six months.
E. Varieties sold in the winter market are stored in the rooms.
questions.explanation: Stored implies keeps six months implies sold in winter. C and E reverse or negate the conditionals; A and D make claims about proportions the statements do not support.

questions.prompt: A university found that students who attend lectures in person achieve higher marks than students who watch the recordings. It is considering making attendance compulsory in order to raise marks.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the proposal?
options: A. Whether the lecture theatres can accommodate all enrolled students
B. How many lectures are recorded each term
C. Whether students prefer attending to watching recordings
D. Whether the difference in marks reflects attendance itself or the characteristics of students who choose to attend
E. What proportion of staff support compulsory attendance
questions.explanation: The proposal only works if attendance is doing the causal work; if organised, well students both attend and score well, compelling the others changes little. A is a genuine constraint on implementation but not on whether marks would rise.

questions.prompt: A streaming service reports that subscribers who use its personalised recommendations watch more hours per month than those who do not, and concludes that the recommendation system increases viewing.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes that hours watched is a good measure of subscriber satisfaction
B. relies on data reported by subscribers themselves
C. fails to distinguish between films and series
D. does not consider the cost of running the system
E. ignores the possibility that subscribers who already watch a great deal are the ones who engage with recommendations
questions.explanation: Heavy viewers have more occasion to use recommendations, so usage may follow viewing rather than cause it. A is a fair objection to the metric but does not address the causal claim.

questions.prompt: A city announced that it had planted two million trees over five years and described the programme as a major contribution to reducing the city's carbon emissions.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the city's description?
options: A. Roughly half the planted trees died within three years, and those surviving will absorb a small fraction of the city's annual emissions for decades.
B. Trees also reduce summer temperatures in built-up areas.
C. The programme cost more than originally budgeted.
D. Some residents objected to the species chosen.
E. Other cities have planted more trees over the same period.
questions.explanation: It attacks both the survival of the plantings and the scale of the effect relative to emissions, which is what the claim of a major contribution requires. C, D and E concern the programme's management or comparison, not its climate effect.

questions.prompt: A hospital reduced the average length of stay on its surgical wards by discharging patients earlier, and reports that this has increased the number of operations it can perform each month. A critic argues that the policy may not have improved the hospital's overall performance.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most supports the critic's position?
options: A. Patients report that they would have preferred to stay longer.
B. Surgical staff work longer hours than before.
C. The proportion of discharged patients readmitted within thirty days has risen by an amount that offsets much of the gain in capacity.
D. The hospital's waiting list remains long.
E. Other hospitals have adopted similar policies.
questions.explanation: Readmissions consume the very capacity the policy released, which is the strongest available challenge to a claim about overall performance. A is about preference, not performance; D is consistent with an improvement that is simply insufficient.

questions.prompt: Recycling aluminium requires about 5 per cent of the energy needed to produce the same quantity from ore. A commentator concludes that a country can reduce the energy used by its aluminium industry by 95 per cent by recycling all the aluminium it uses.
questions.question: The commentator's reasoning is flawed because it
options: A. overlooks the energy used in transporting scrap aluminium
B. assumes that the quantity of aluminium available for recycling is sufficient to meet demand
C. ignores the value of aluminium as a commodity
D. confuses energy use with carbon emissions
E. relies on figures from a single industry study
questions.explanation: Demand grows and metal remains in use for decades, so scrap available in any year is far less than consumption; the remainder must still come from ore. A is a real but second-order cost.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to pay football referees a full-time salary argue that professional referees make fewer errors than part-time ones. Opponents note that the leagues employing full-time referees are also the wealthiest, and use more video review technology than other leagues.
questions.question: The opponents' response functions in the argument by
options: A. denying that referees make errors
B. questioning the reliability of the data on refereeing errors
C. arguing that the cost of full-time salaries is prohibitive
D. proposing an alternative method of training referees
E. identifying a factor that could account for the difference the supporters attribute to full-time employment
questions.explanation: The response supplies a confounding variable — video review — that could produce the observed difference without any effect of employment status. It neither denies the data nor argues about cost.

questions.passageText:
A shopping centre charges its anchor store a low rent and its small tenants a high one; a newspaper sells copies below the cost of printing them and recovers the difference from advertisers; a card network charges merchants and, in many countries, pays cardholders. In each case a firm serves two groups whose demand depends on the other's participation, and the striking feature is that the price to one side may be set below cost, or below zero, without any predatory intent.

The logic is that the value each side receives rises with the number of users on the other. If cardholders are numerous, merchants will accept the card; if merchants accept it, cardholders will carry it. A platform that ignored this and priced each side at its own cost of service would attract too few users on the more price-sensitive side and, in consequence, too few on the other.

Which side is subsidised follows from three factors: relative price sensitivity, the strength of the benefit each side confers on the other, and the extent to which users of one side deal with several platforms at once. Newspapers subsidise readers because advertisers value readers more than readers value advertisements.

The analytical difficulty this creates for competition authorities is substantial. A price below cost on one side, which in an ordinary market is evidence of an attempt to drive out rivals, may here be the ordinary competitive outcome. Assessing conduct requires looking at both sides together, and courts that have examined only the side where the complaint arose have reached conclusions that the structure of the market does not support.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that a platform may price below cost on one side because
options: A. it intends to drive competitors out of the market
B. regulators require access at low prices
C. the value to each side rises with the number of users on the other
D. costs on that side are difficult to measure
E. the subsidised side is more profitable in the long run
questions.explanation: The cross-side effect is the stated logic; the passage explicitly contrasts it with predatory intent. E is not claimed — the subsidised side may never become profitable on its own.

options: A. compare a platform's prices with those of firms in ordinary markets
B. rely on evidence from other jurisdictions
C. treat advertising revenue as a cost

questions.passageText:
Antibiotic resistance is usually explained by a simple model: exposure to a drug kills susceptible bacteria and leaves resistant ones to multiply, so reducing exposure should allow susceptible strains to reclaim the population. The model rests on an assumption — that resistance carries a fitness cost, making resistant bacteria worse competitors in the absence of the drug.

That assumption is often true and reliably incomplete. Resistance mechanisms do impose costs: producing an enzyme that degrades a drug consumes resources, and an altered target protein may perform its original function less well. Where the cost is substantial, withdrawal of a drug is followed by a decline in resistance, and several national programmes have observed exactly that.

The complication is compensatory evolution. Bacteria acquire secondary mutations that offset the cost without abandoning the resistance, and such mutations are common because the population sizes involved are enormous. Once compensation has occurred, resistance may persist indefinitely after the selecting drug is withdrawn, and the reversal that policy assumes does not arrive.

Two further factors work in the same direction. Resistance genes frequently travel on plasmids carrying several resistance genes together, so use of one drug can maintain resistance to others that are no longer used. And the environments in which resistant bacteria live are not drug-free: agricultural, industrial and household biocides can select for the same genes.

The practical implication is not that reducing antibiotic use is pointless. It is that the benefit should be expected to appear as a slower rise rather than as a return to a previous state, and that policies promising reversal are promising something the biology does not generally deliver.
questions.prompt: The 'simple model' described in the first paragraph assumes that
options: A. resistance genes are carried on plasmids
B. resistance imposes a fitness cost, so resistant bacteria compete poorly without the drug
C. bacteria cannot acquire secondary mutations
D. antibiotic use in agriculture is negligible
E. susceptible bacteria reproduce faster than resistant ones under any conditions
questions.explanation: The passage names the assumption explicitly. C and D are complications introduced later, not the model's stated premise; E overstates the assumption, which concerns the drug-free case.

options: A. are worthwhile but should not be expected to return resistance to earlier levels
B. should be abandoned as ineffective
C. will succeed only if applied to agriculture as well as medicine

questions.passageText:
Randomised controlled trials have reshaped development economics. By assigning a programme to some communities and not others, a trial removes the selection problems that make observational comparisons hard to interpret, and answers with unusual credibility the question of what happened where the trial was run.

The last clause is the whole of the controversy. Internal validity — confidence that the measured effect was caused by the intervention — is what randomisation buys. External validity, the applicability of the result elsewhere, it does not buy at all. A programme that raised school attendance in one district may fail in another because the constraint that bound in the first place was not the constraint that binds in the second.

Defenders answer that this is a problem for every method, not for trials in particular, and that the correct response is replication across contexts plus theory about the mechanism. Critics reply that scarce funds have been directed toward questions that are tractable by trial rather than questions that matter most, and that important subjects — trade policy, exchange rate regimes, the design of institutions — cannot be randomised at all and risk being neglected because of it.

A more measured position has emerged. A trial answers a narrow question well, and its result becomes portable only when combined with an account of why the effect occurred and evidence that the same conditions hold elsewhere. On that view the method's characteristic failure is not a false result but a true result carried further than it can bear.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, randomisation secures
options: A. both internal and external validity
B. external validity but not internal validity
C. internal validity but not external validity
D. neither, unless the sample is very large
E. validity only where the intervention is inexpensive
questions.explanation: The passage draws exactly this distinction and says randomisation does not buy external validity at all.

questions.passageText:
The metal shipping container is often described as an invention, but its components were unremarkable. What was difficult was agreement. A container is useful only if it fits the ships, cranes, lorries and railway wagons of everyone the cargo will pass through, and in the 1950s each operator had its own dimensions and fittings.

Standardisation therefore had to be negotiated among parties with conflicting interests. Firms that had already invested in a particular size lobbied for it, since a rival's standard would strand their assets. The corner fitting that allows containers to be lifted and locked was patented; the resulting arrangement, in which the patent holder licensed it without royalty in exchange for its adoption as the standard, is a case study in what a firm will surrender to make its own equipment universal.

The economic effects were not immediate. For roughly a decade after the first container voyage, savings were modest, because the benefit required ports, railways and warehouses to be rebuilt around the box. When the gains did arrive they were large and diffuse: dock labour requirements collapsed, port cities that failed to invest lost traffic permanently to those that did, and the cost of moving manufactured goods fell far enough to make it economic to produce components on one continent and assemble them on another.

The history is a corrective to accounts that treat technical invention as the moment of change. The box was simple; the institutional work of making everyone use the same box, and of rebuilding the world's ports around it, took twenty years and explains the delay.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the principal obstacle to containerisation was
options: A. the engineering of a sufficiently strong box
B. a shortage of steel in the 1950s
C. resistance from shipping customers
D. the absence of suitable ships
E. reaching agreement on common dimensions and fittings among parties with conflicting interests
questions.explanation: The passage says the components were unremarkable and that what was difficult was agreement.

options: A. Shipping firms were slow to order new vessels.

Once compensation has occurred, resistance may persist indefinitely after the selecting drug is withdrawn, and the reversal that policy assumes does not arrive.

Two further factors work in the same direction. Resistance genes frequently travel on plasmids carrying several resistance genes together, so use of one drug can maintain resistance to others that are no longer used. And the environments in which resistant bacteria live are not drug-free: agricultural, industrial and household biocides can select for the same genes.

The practical implication is not that reducing antibiotic use is pointless. It is that the benefit should be expected to appear as a slower rise rather than as a return to a previous state, and that policies promising reversal are promising something the biology does not generally deliver.

readingPassages.title: Trials and Their Limits
readingPassages.text:
Randomised controlled trials have reshaped development economics. By assigning a programme to some communities and not others, a trial removes the selection problems that make observational comparisons hard to interpret, and answers with unusual credibility the question of what happened where the trial was run.

The last clause is the whole of the controversy. Internal validity — confidence that the measured effect was caused by the intervention — is what randomisation buys. External validity, the applicability of the result elsewhere, it does not buy at all. A programme that raised school attendance in one district may fail in another because the constraint that bound in the first place was not the constraint that binds in the second.

Defenders answer that this is a problem for every method, not for trials in particular, and that the correct response is replication across contexts plus theory about the mechanism. Critics reply that scarce funds have been directed toward questions that are tractable by trial rather than questions that matter most, and that important subjects — trade policy, exchange rate regimes, the design of institutions — cannot be randomised at all and risk being neglected because of it.

A more measured position has emerged. A trial answers a narrow question well, and its result becomes portable only when combined with an account of why the effect occurred and evidence that the same conditions hold elsewhere. On that view the method's characteristic failure is not a false result but a true result carried further than it can bear.

readingPassages.title: The Container
readingPassages.text:
The metal shipping container is often described as an invention, but its components were unremarkable. What was difficult was agreement. A container is useful only if it fits the ships, cranes, lorries and railway wagons of everyone the cargo will pass through, and in the 1950s each operator had its own dimensions and fittings.

Standardisation therefore had to be negotiated among parties with conflicting interests. Firms that had already invested in a particular size lobbied for it, since a rival's standard would strand their assets. The corner fitting that allows containers to be lifted and locked was patented; the resulting arrangement, in which the patent holder licensed it without royalty in exchange for its adoption as the standard, is a case study in what a firm will surrender to make its own equipment universal.

The economic effects were not immediate. For roughly a decade after the first container voyage, savings were modest, because the benefit required ports, railways and warehouses to be rebuilt around the box. When the gains did arrive they were large and diffuse: dock labour requirements collapsed, port cities that failed to invest lost traffic permanently to those that did, and the cost of moving manufactured goods fell far enough to make it economic to produce components on one continent and assemble them on another.

The history is a corrective to accounts that treat technical invention as the moment of change. The box was simple; the institutional work of making everyone use the same box, and of rebuilding the world's ports around it, took twenty years and explains the delay.
